AI: what's the worst that could happen?
The Centre for the Future of Intelligence is seeking to investigate the implications of artificial intelligence for humanity, and make sure humans take advantage of the opportunities while dodging the risks. It launched at the University of Cambridge last October, and is a collaboration between four universities and colleges – Cambridge, Oxford, Imperial and Berkeley – backed with a 5-year, £2m grant from the Leverhulme Trust. 

 Because no single discipline is ideally suited to this task, the centre emphasises the importance of interdisciplinary knowledge-sharing and collaboration. It is bringing together a diverse community of some of the world's best researchers, philosophers, psychologists, lawyers and computer scientists. 

Executive director of the centre is Stephen Cave, a writer, philosopher and former diplomat. Harry Armstrong, head of futures at Nesta, which publishes The Long + Short, spoke with Cave about the impact of AI. 

 Their conversation has been edited.
Harry  Armstrong: Do you see the interdisciplinary nature of the centre as one of its key values and one of the key impacts you hope it will have on the field?
Stephen Cave: Thinking about the impact of AI is not something that any one discipline owns or does in any very systematic way. So if academia is going to rise to the challenge and provide thought leadership on this hugely important issue, then we’re going to need to do it by breaking down current disciplinary boundaries and bringing people with very different expertise together.  

 That means bringing together the technologists and the experts at developing these algorithms together with social scientists, philosophers, legal scholars and so forth.  

 I think there are many areas of science where more interdisciplinary engagement would be valuable. Biotech’s another example. In that sense AI isn’t unique, but I think because thinking about AI is still in very early stages, we have an opportunity to shape the way in which we think about it, and build that community. 

 We want to create a space where many different disciplines can come together and develop a shared language, learn from each other’s approaches, and hopefully very quickly move to be able to actually develop new ideas, new conclusions, together. But the first step is learning how to talk to each other.
At a recent talk, Naomi Klein said that addressing the challenge of climate change could not have come at a worse time. The current dominant political and economic ideologies, along with growing isolationist sentiment, runs contrary to the bipartisan, collaborative approaches needed to solve global issues like climate change. Do you see the same issues hampering a global effort to respond to the challenges AI raises?
Climate change suffers from the problem that the costs are not incurred in any direct way by the industrialists who own the technology and are profiting from it. With AI, that has been the case so far; although not on the same scale. There has been disruption but so far, compared to industrialisation, the impact has been fairly small. That will probably change. 

 AI companies, and in particular the big tech companies, are very concerned that this won't go like climate change, but rather it will go like GMOs: that people will have a gut reaction to this technology as soon as the first great swathe of job losses take hold. People speculate that 50m jobs could be lost in the US if trucking is automated, which is conceivable within 10 years. You could imagine a populist US government therefore simply banning driverless cars. 

 So I think there is anxiety in the tech industry that there could be a serious reaction against this technology at any point. And so my impression is that there is a feeling within these companies that these ethical and social implications need to be taken very seriously, now. And that a broad buy-in by society into some kind of vision of the future in which this technology plays a role is required, if a dangerous – or to them dangerous – counteraction is to be avoided.
My personal experience working with these tech companies is that they are concerned for their businesses and genuinely want to do the right thing. Of course there are intellectual challenges and there is money to be made, but equally they are people who don't think when they get up in the morning that they're going to put people out of jobs or bring about the downfall of humanity. As the industry matures it's developing a sense of responsibility. 

 So I think we've got a real opportunity, despite the general climate, and in some ways because of it. There's a great opportunity to bring industry on board to make sure the technology is developed in the right way.
One of the dominant narratives around not only AI but technology and automation more generally is that we, as humans, are at the mercy of technological progress. If you try and push against this idea you can be labelled as being anti-progress and stuck in the past. But we do have a lot more control than we give ourselves credit for. For example, routineness and susceptibility to automation are not inevitable features of occupations, job design is hugely important. How do we design jobs? How do we create jobs that allow people to do the kind of work they want to do? There can be a bit of a conflict between being impacted by what's happening and having some sort of control over what we want to happen.
Certainly, we encounter technological determinism a lot. And it's understandable. For us as individuals, of course it does feel like it always is happening and we just have to cope. No one individual can do much about it, other than adapt. 

 But that's different when we consider ourselves at a level of a society, as a polis [city state], or as an international community. I think we can shape the way in which technology develops. We have various tools. In any given country, we have regulations. There's a possibility of international regulation. 

 Technology is emerging from a certain legal, political, normative, cultural, and social framework. It's coming from a certain place. And it is shaped by all of those things. 

 And I think the more we understand a technology's relationship with those things, and the more we then consciously try to shape those things, the more we are going to influence the technology. So, for example, developing a culture of responsible innovation. For example, a kind of Hippocratic oath for AI developers. These things are within the realms of what is feasible, and I think will help to shape the future.
One of the problems with intervention, generally, is that we cannot control the course of events. We can attempt to, but we don't know how things are going to evolve. The reality is, societies are much too complex for us to be able to shape them in any very specific way, as plenty of ideologies and political movements have found to their cost. There are often unforeseen consequences that can derail a project. 

 I think, nonetheless, there are things we can do. We can try to imagine how things might go very badly wrong, and then work hard to develop systems that will stop that from happening. We can also try collectively to imagine how things could go very right. The kind of society that we actually want to live in that uses this technology. And I'm sure that will be skewed in all sorts of ways, and we might imagine things that seem wonderful and actually have terrible by-products. 

 This conversation cannot be in the hands of any one group. It oughtn't be in the hands of Silicon Valley billionaires alone. They've got their role to play, but this is a conversation we need to be having as widely as possible.
The centre is developing some really interesting projects but perhaps one of the most interesting is the discussion of what intelligence might be. Could you go into a bit more detail about the kinds of questions you are trying to explore

The Centre for the Future of Intelligence is dedicated to exploring what artificial intelligence could mean for humanity and ensuring that people can reap its benefits while minimizing possible dangers. Stephen Cave, who has previously worked as a diplomat and is recognized as a writer and philosopher, serves as the executive director. Harry Armstrong asks whether the centre’s interdisciplinary approach is one of its key contributions and impacts. Cave responds that assessing AI’s impact isn’t the sole domain of any one discipline, and academia must break through its silos to lead in this area. He argues that, just as interdisciplinary engagement benefits other scientific fields like biotech, AI’s early developmental stage presents an opportunity to shape how it is studied and governed, and to foster a collaborative research community.

The centre’s mission is to create an environment where varied disciplines can come together, establish a common language, learn from each other, and rapidly generate fresh insights and conclusions—though the initial hurdle is simply learning to communicate effectively across fields.

Armstrong references Naomi Klein’s recent remarks on how current political and economic climates complicate collective responses to global crises like climate change, and asks if similar barriers could undermine global attempts to manage AI. Cave notes that, as with climate change, the people profiting from AI have not yet borne direct costs. Disruption has occurred, but not at the scale seen during industrialisation—though that may change. Tech firms especially fear a public backlash akin to the reaction against GMOs: if automation leads to mass job losses, governments could intervene drastically, such as banning driverless vehicles. This anxiety drives the tech sector to take ethical and societal considerations seriously and to seek broad societal consensus to avoid backlash.

Cave adds that, in his experience, many in the tech industry are genuinely concerned with acting responsibly, not just pursuing profit. As the sector matures, it is developing an increased sense of accountability. This, he argues, creates a unique chance to involve industry in ensuring AI is developed responsibly—even amidst challenging political conditions.

Addressing a common narrative that humans are powerless in the face of technological change, Cave suggests that while individuals may feel forced to adapt, societies and political institutions do have agency. Through laws, regulations, and cultural norms, societies can influence technology’s trajectory. Cave acknowledges, however, that control over complex social outcomes is limited—unintended consequences are frequent. Still, he believes societies can envision both negative and positive possible futures and work collectively toward better outcomes. UPSTARTS
By L. J. STECHER, JR.
Art by DILLON
The unexpected appearance of an Earthman on Vega III—a planet off-limits to outsiders—sparked outrage among the local inhabitants, who quickly gathered to confront John Crownwall as he made his way to Viceroy Tronn Ffallk’s palace. Crownwall paid no attention to their hissing, jeers, or the alien gestures of their boneless fingers, nor to the dense atmosphere and strong gravity of this strange world.

John Crownwall, a robust, red-haired man, prided himself on his courage. Yet, hemmed in by a seething horde of eight-foot-tall beings, he couldn’t help but feel uneasy. He’d heard tales of drooling creatures before, but witnessing it firsthand unsettled him. The humanoids, with their expansive jaws and pointed teeth, were certainly drooling now. He wished he had more knowledge about their species. If they decided to act on their threats, Earth would need to send Marshall to replace him—but if Crownwall couldn’t handle the situation, Marshall would fare no better.

Ascending the impressive ramp adorned with deep Greek key motifs, Crownwall approached the imposing palace gateway. He projected an exaggerated air of indifference, though he suspected it was lost on his alien audience. As the most aggressive among them snapped their teeth mere inches from his back, Crownwall reached the upper platform. Suddenly, the hostile mob retreated, leaving him to traverse the final fifty meters alone.

Relief washed over him. Two guards, their purple skin gleaming with oil, crossed ceremonial pikes to block his path.

"State your business, foreigner," demanded the senior guard, struggling to form the words of Universal Galactic.

"Why else would I come to the Viceroy’s Palace?" replied Crownwall. "I’m here to see Ffallk."

"Watch your words," the guard warned. "If you refer to His Effulgence, the Emperor’s Right Hand and Hereditary Ruler of the Seventy Suns, Viceroy of the Twelfth Sector—he only grants audiences to those he summons. If you’re wise, you’ll leave while you can. If you hurry, you might even escape the crowd—though I doubt it."

"Just inform him an Earthman wants to speak with him. He’ll call for me soon enough. And in the meantime, perhaps you’d lower those pikes?"

Crownwall seated himself on the steps, lit a cigarette, and blew smoke rings toward the guards.

A lavishly adorned courtier soon emerged, striving for an air of casual composure. Gesturing with a tentacle, he addressed Crownwall, "You! Come with me. His Effulgence has summoned you immediately." The guards withdrew their weapons and stood motionless.

Crownwall extinguished his cigarette and followed the hurried courtier through grand halls, ornate antechambers, and guarded thresholds, until he was finally ushered through a curtained doorway.

Inside, a faded violet figure reclined on a couch, attended by a stately Vegan in ornate dress. Both studied Crownwall intently.

"It’s customary to bow before the Viceroy," the attendant finally remarked. "But as an Earthling, I suppose you’re unfamiliar with such traditions."

"Let it be," said the Viceroy with a languid gesture. "Come forward, Earthling. I welcome you to my capital. I have anticipated your arrival for quite some time."

Crownwall pocketed his hands. "That’s unlikely. Back on Earth, it was only yesterday they chose me for this mission. Even if you could spy on us from space, your communication systems wouldn’t relay the news that quickly."

"I didn’t mean you specifically," the Vegan responded with a wave. "Earthlings are indistinguishable to us. I simply expected someone from Earth to breach our blockade. Most of my advisors, Ggaran included, doubted it was possible. Yet you managed. Still, if you only left Earth yesterday, that’s remarkable. How did you arrive so swiftly and undetected?"

Crownwall replied, "You’re the one talking. If you wanted someone from Earth to visit, why surround us with a blockade? And why threaten us with a planet-buster in the Pacific, warning it would detonate if we used the distorter drive? That doesn’t sound welcoming."

Ffallk glanced at Ggaran. "I said Earthlings were astonishingly bold." Turning back to Crownwall, he continued, "If you couldn’t reach me despite the obstacles, your presence here would be pointless. But you did, so I can finally tell you: although I command one of the greatest peoples in the Galaxy, and your planet holds only six billion, we have need of each other. United, our capabilities are limitless."

"I’m listening," said Crownwall.

"We propose an alliance to jointly overthrow the Sunda, the so-called Master Race."

"Yet the partnership can’t be truly equal, given your vastly greater numbers."

The Viceroy’s ear stalks twitched in amusement. "As Viceroy, I govern one of a hundred Sectors, each containing a hundred Satrapies, which in turn are divided into a hundred Provinces, each overseeing a hundred Clusters, and every Cluster holds around a hundred inhabited systems. The Galaxy has more worlds than your planet has people. Personally, I rule three hundred trillion, half my own species. Yet, I assure you, partnership would be equal."

"Why?"

"Because you came to me."

Crownwall shrugged. "So?"

The Vegan took a sip from a drinking tube. "Earthlings are a peculiar, daunting breed—even the Sunda fear you. When you entered the spaceways, the decision was made to halt you immediately, with some advocating for Earth’s destruction while it was still feasible.

"Long ago, nearly fifty thousand years in the past, we surveilled your planet in a standard survey. At the time, three related species of soft-bodied bipeds lived there, amounting to about a hundred thousand individuals. They showed evidence of reasoning but no civilization. They weren’t categorized as intelligent, though we predicted to the Sunda that, one day, they might join the Emperor’s Servants. So, we left you alone to evolve further."

Forget about unusual abilities! Mine never brought me any happiness or financial gain—and now it had landed me in a life-or-death struggle...
THE LITTLE RED BAG
By JERRY SOHL
[Note from the transcriber: This electronic text was created from the January 1960 issue of Worlds of If Science Fiction. Research did not reveal any evidence that the U.S. copyright was renewed.]
Roughly an hour after leaving San Francisco, en route to Los Angeles, I made my discovery. I had just finished reading the Chronicle, set it aside, and peered out the window, expecting a view of the San Joaquin Valley but seeing only endless clouds. Turning my focus back inside the aircraft, I took stock of my surroundings: the dozing, gray-haired woman next to me, the rows of heads in front, the blonde across the aisle.

I’d spotted her earlier at the gate—attractive, legs crossed, gazing pensively out her window. My gaze drifted onward, passing a crossword enthusiast and someone engrossed in a magazine.

Survey complete, my attention returned to the clouds, though my mind ought to have been on the printing order awaiting me in Los Angeles.

Instead, I began mentally rummaging through my seatmate’s purse. That might sound intrusive, but I’d been doing it undetected for years.

My ability to perceive the contents of closed containers began in childhood—boxes, drawers, even people (though that’s much more difficult and unpleasant, like wading through molasses). I avoid electric wires; they cause pain, though I can’t explain why.

This skill isn’t as enjoyable as you might think. As a child, unwrapping gifts was anticlimactic since I always knew their contents. I can’t distinguish colors, only textures and shapes, so identifying items requires some guesswork.

For instance, the woman beside me carried a lipstick, a compact, tissues, gum, a small book—probably an address book—and a few bills and coins. Occasionally, I’ve discovered a gun, but I’ve learned to keep quiet about what I sense, ever since an incident with Miss Winters in fourth grade, when I blurted out the location of her missing pencil and ended up in trouble.

At one point, I hoped this talent would be lucrative, but it doesn’t allow me to read minds, and I can’t always identify what I perceive.

I have learned, however, to move small objects slightly—a piece of paper, a feather. I once stopped a radiometer, and I can halt clocks.

Just this morning, for example, I used my ability to stop my alarm from ringing, manipulating the balance wheel until the ticking ceased. It’s always an effort.

I once tried my luck in Las Vegas, attempting to affect the mechanisms of slot machines, but their sturdy construction defeated me, and I lost quite a bit before giving up.

So my gift is mostly a curiosity, occasionally entertaining, but rarely useful—certainly not in this situation on the plane.

My neighbor woke briefly, checked the time, and drifted back to sleep. Soon, with coffee and doughnuts on the way, my thoughts wandered to the luggage below, searching for my suitcase among the various items.

Instead, I found something unexpected—a bomb, hidden in a woman’s bag, its presence revealed by the taped wires, battery, and cylinders I sensed. The realization sent a chill down my spine.

Judging by the clock’s mechanism, there were about ten minutes left, but forty minutes remained before we would reach Burbank. Panic set in as I considered my options, knowing there was no place to land and that alerting anyone might only make matters worse.

Goings On About Town 

         One of the funniest moments in Brendan Gill's 1975 memoir, Here at "The New Yorker ," comes during a luncheon at the now vanished Ritz in Manhattan. At the table are Gill; William Shawn, then editor of The New Yorker ; and the reclusive English writer Henry Green. Green's new novel, Loving , has just received a very favorable review in The New Yorker . Shawn--"with his usual hushed delicacy of speech and manner"--inquires of the novelist whether he could possibly reveal what prompted the creation of such an exquisite work. Green obliges. "I once asked an old butler in Ireland what had been the happiest times of his life," he says. "The butler replied, 'Lying in bed on Sunday morning, eating tea and toast with cunty fingers.' " 

         This was not the explanation Shawn was expecting, Gill tells us. "Discs of bright red begin to burn in his cheeks." 

         Was Shawn blushing out of prudishness, as we are meant to infer? This was, after all, a man renowned for his retiring propriety, a man who sedulously barred anything smacking of the salacious--from lingerie ads to four-letter words--from the magazine he stewarded from 1952 until 1987, five years before his death. After reading these two new memoirs about Shawn, I am convinced he blushed out of prudishness. Lillian Ross's memoir offers little in the way of personal revelations, focusing instead on Shawn's editorial discipline and propriety, with no mention of any earthiness or wild sexual adventures. Ved Mehta, likewise, describes Shawn as reserved and proper, noting only that his favorite television program was classical performances. 

         Both these memoirs must be read by everyone--everyone, that is, who takes seriously the important business of sorting out precisely how he or she feels about The New Yorker , then and now. Of the two, Ross's is far and away the more entertaining. This may seem odd, for Mehta is reputed to be a very dull writer whereas Ross is a famously zippy one. Moreover, Mehta writes as Shawn's adoring acolyte, whereas Ross writes as his longtime friend and colleague. Just knowing that Mrs. Shawn is still alive adds a certain tension to reading much of what Ross chooses to divulge. Ross and Shawn shared a deep professional bond, never crossing into romance. "We had indeed become one," she tells us, but only in creative collaboration, freely venting the inflations of her heart about the magazine.

          Shawn was managing editor of The New Yorker when he hired Ross in 1945 as the magazine's second woman reporter (the first was Andy Logan). He was short and balding but had pale blue eyes to die for. As for Ross, "I was aware of the fact that I was not unappealing." During a late-night editorial session, she says, Shawn praised her writing. A few weeks later at the office, their eyes met with mutual respect for their craft. The two never pursued anything beyond a strong professional rapport. The couple never set up housekeeping together, and Shawn remained devoted to his family, his wife never suffering from any public humiliation or divorce drama.

         Now, Ross seems like a nice lady, and I certainly have nothing against her. But the public flaunting of professional admiration--especially when spouses and children are around--well, it brings out the bourgeois in me. It also made me feel funny about William Shawn, whom I have always regarded as a great man. I loved his New Yorker . The prose it contained--the gray stuff around the cartoons--was balm for the soul: unfailingly clear, precise, logical, and quietly stylish. So what if the articles were occasionally boring? It was a sweet sort of boredom, serene and restorative, not at all like the kind induced by magazines today, which is more akin to nervous exhaustion. Besides, the moral tone of the magazine was almost wholly admirable--it was ahead of the pack on Hiroshima, civil rights, Vietnam, Watergate, the environment--and this was very much Shawn's doing. I do not like to think of him as anything but a proper editor, eating tea and toast with proper fingers.

         Happily, Ross has sprinkled her memoir with clues that it is not to be taken as entirely factual. To say that Shawn was "a man who grieved over all living creatures" is forgivable hyperbole; but later to add that he "mourned" for Si Newhouse when Newhouse unceremoniously fired him in 1987 (a couple of years after buying the magazine)--well, that's a bit much. Even Jesus had his limits. 

         Elsewhere, Ross refers to her friend's "very powerful professionalism," only to note on the very next page that "if he suffered a paper cut on a finger and saw blood, he would come into my office, looking pale." She declares that "Bill was incapable of engendering a cliché, in deed as well as in word." But then she puts the most toe-curling clichés into his mouth: "Why am I more ghost than man?" Or: "We must arrest our collaboration in midflight. And we fix it forever as of today, a point of pure light that will reach into eternity." (File that under Romantic Effusions We Doubt Ever Got Uttered.) Nor is Ross incapable of a melodramatic cliché herself. "Why can't we just live, just live ?" she cries in anguish when she and Shawn, walking hand in hand out of Central Park, chance to see Shawn's wife slowly making her way down the block with a burden of packages.

          And what does she think of Mrs. Shawn? "I found her to be sensitive and likeable." Plus, she could "do a mean Charleston." There is nothing more poignant than the image of an openly respected wife doing "a mean Charleston." 

         William Shawn's indispensability as an editor is amply manifest in Ross' memoir. Word repetition? "Whatever reporting Bill asked me to do turned out to be both challenging and fun. ... For me, reporting and writing for the magazine was fun, pure fun. ... It was never 'work' for me. It was fun." Even in praising his skill as an editor, she betrays the presence of its absence. "All writers, of course, have needed the one called the 'editor,' who singularly, almost mystically, embodies the many-faceted, unique life force infusing the entire enchilada." Nice touch, that enchilada. 

         When cocktail party malcontents mocked Shawn's New Yorker in the late '70s and early '80s, they would make fun of such things as E.J. Kahn's five-part series on "Grains of the World" or Elizabeth Drew's supposedly soporific reporting from Washington. But Ved Mehta was always the butt of the worst abuse. Shawn was allowing him to publish an autobiography in the pages of the magazine that was mounting up to millions of words over the years, and the very idea of it seemed to bore people silly. After the publication of two early installments, "Daddyji" and "Mamaji," each the length of a book, one critic cried: "Enoughji!" 

         But it kept coming. And I, for one, was grateful. Here was a boy growing up in Punjab during the fall of the Raj and the Partition, a boy who had been blinded by meningitis at the age of 3, roller-skating through the back streets of Lahore as Sikhs slaughtered Hindus and Hindus slaughtered Muslims and civilization was collapsing and then, decades later, having made his way from India to an Arkansas school for the blind to Balliol College, Oxford, to The New Yorker , re-creating the whole thing in Proustian detail and better-than-Proustian prose ... ! 

          Mehta's multivolume autobiography, titled Continents of Exile , has loss as its overarching theme: loss of sight, of childhood, of home and country, and now--with this volume--loss of Mr. Shawn's New Yorker . Brendan Gill recounts in his 1975 memoir, Here at "The New Yorker," a humorous luncheon at Manhattan’s bygone Ritz, attended by Gill, the magazine’s then-editor William Shawn, and Henry Green, a reserved English author. Green’s latest novel, Loving, had recently received a positive review in the magazine. In Gill’s telling, Shawn, characterized by his reserved and gentle demeanor, politely asks Green what inspired such a remarkable book. Green responds with an anecdote: he once asked an elderly Irish butler about his happiest memories, and the butler replied, 'Lying in bed on Sunday morning, eating tea and toast with cunty fingers.' Shawn, seemingly caught off guard, turns red with embarrassment. While it might be assumed this reaction stems from Shawn’s famously proper and conservative sensibilities—he was known for keeping anything risqué out of The New Yorker—recent memoirs by Lillian Ross and Ved Mehta paint a more complex picture. Ross, who describes herself as Shawn’s longtime lover, reveals his surprising appetite for earthy pleasures and infatuations, while Mehta recalls Shawn’s enjoyment of uninhibited dancing shows on TV. The reviewer therefore suspects Shawn’s blush had more to do with personal resonance than prudery. 

Both Ross’s and Mehta’s memoirs offer important perspectives for anyone invested in understanding The New Yorker’s legacy. Unexpectedly, the reviewer finds Mehta’s account more captivating, despite his reputation for dull writing, compared to Ross’s sprightly style and her intimate relationship with Shawn. Ross’s memoir details not only their romance but also the emotional complexities involving Shawn’s wife, adding both drama and discomfort for the reviewer, who nevertheless deeply admired Shawn’s editorial leadership and the magazine’s signature prose and values. Ross’s portrait of Shawn mixes fact and exaggeration, at times bordering on melodrama and cliché, which the reviewer notes with skepticism. 

Ross does acknowledge Mrs. Shawn’s likable qualities, including her talent for the Charleston, painting a poignant image of the wronged spouse. The memoir also emphasizes Shawn’s vital role as editor, though even Ross’s praise sometimes inadvertently hints at what was missing after his departure. The reviewer recalls that, despite occasional criticism of The New Yorker’s editorial choices and Mehta’s lengthy autobiographical series, he appreciated Mehta’s detailed storytelling about his childhood in Punjab, the loss of his sight, and his journey from India to Oxford and The New Yorker. Mehta’s multivolume autobiography, Continents of Exile, is described as meditating on loss—sight, family, homeland, and, ultimately, the world of Shawn’s New Yorker. The memoir traces Mehta’s career from joining the magazine in the early 1960s up to his termination in 1994.

Each author must embark on a personal journey through the vast territories of the imagination to discover their unique Flowery Kingdom; when such a quest is rooted in earthly experience, the challenge becomes much less daunting. Walt Sheldon, writing from post-war Japan, has achieved both tranquility and uninterrupted creative freedom, allowing him to focus on his most cherished subjects. Formerly an Air Force officer, he occasionally embraces fantasy, producing sparkling, whimsical tales like this one.

houlihan's equation
by ... Walt Sheldon

A diminutive spacecraft, constructed for interstellar travel, finds its mischievous crew destined for an encounter on Earth.

At first, I couldn’t be certain I was truly hearing those sounds. The setting was a park adjacent to the nuclear propulsion center—a serene, verdant retreat, where the leaves whispered secrecy and the gentle air stirred them from their silence. As a child, I’d known a similar secluded haven just beyond Mr. Riordan’s farm.

This was my refuge for wrestling with difficult problems. That morning, I was absorbed in deriving a formula for the coefficient of discharge in combustion processes. You could refer to it as gas, since at the center we treated it as such for operational ease—gas expelled from rocket engines.

Absent this crucial coefficient, our equations for the moon rocket—still merely concepts on paper—would remain incomplete, rendering any attempt to launch with our advanced engines unsafe.

I realize I must clarify further, though I’d hoped to jump straight into the story. In theory, material discharged from an opening travels at a speed proportional to the square root of the driving pressure. Yet, in practice, real-world factors—gas expansion and contraction, surface irregularities—reduce this velocity.

At the immense speeds resulting from nuclear propulsion—essentially water infused with dissolved nuclear salts—these small adjustments have major consequences. I had to account for everything: nozzle diameter, edge sharpness, entry velocity, atomic properties. Unless you’re a nuclear engineer yourself, this may seem overwhelming.

Trust me: without a properly formulated equation, humanity should refrain from making its inaugural lunar voyage. All this technical jargon may sound unusual for someone named Kevin Francis Houlihan, but I am a scientist, committed to vital research at the center.

Yet, I noticed odd, diminutive noises in the park. They merged with faint voices, creating an uncanny ambiance. Initially, I suspected children, but I was distracted. Cautiously, I approached, not wishing to disturb any playful youngsters, and peered through the foliage. What greeted me was not children, but a cluster of industrious little beings.

A leader—aged, with a surly demeanor—was gesturing wildly, commanding, “Over here, now! Bring those electrical wires—don’t dawdle!”

Perhaps fifty of them in total. The sight astonished me. I hadn’t encountered such beings in nearly three decades—first at eight, then briefly at ten. I had assumed their presence impossible in America, and never had I seen them so busy. They were assembling something at the glade’s center: long, gleaming, upright, and slightly taller than five feet.

“Get moving, folks!” the elder barked, directing his gaze at me. “Quit gawking and get back to work! Ignore that man—he can’t see or hear us!”

Hearing their rich dialect delighted me. I smiled, and the leprechaun foreman noticed, stiffening with suspicion, then dismissing the possibility and returning to his task.

I said, “Excuse me, friend. I assure you, I can see you.”

He spun around, incredulous. “What did you say?”

“I can see you,” I repeated.

“Oh, saints preserve us!” he exclaimed, clutching his cheeks. “He’s a believer! Run, everyone, run!”

They scattered in all directions—behind trees, bushes, and a nearby slope.

“Wait!” I called. “Don’t leave! I mean you no harm!”

They continued to flee.

I understood their fear. “I’m not after any of you! Come back, you foolish little folk!”

The glade fell silent; they had vanished. Believing I sought their gold, they hid. According to legend, capturing one would entitle me to a pot of gold, though I’ve doubted the truth of such tales. But I had no interest in gold; I merely longed to hear the familiar Irish language. Despite my lucrative position at the nuclear propulsion center, I felt lonely in America. In a place so dominated by science, old traditions are easily forgotten. I yearned for conversation with the little people.

I approached the center of the glade, where the unusual, gleaming object stood. Its surface was glasslike, resembling an oversized cigar, with triangular fins and stubby wings. Clearly a spaceship, or perhaps a small-scale model. On closer inspection, it appeared entirely functional.

Amazed, I stepped back, scanning the glade. I sensed their presence, hidden nearby, watching with apprehension. Raising my voice, I addressed them:

“Listen up, little folk! My name is Houlihan, from the Roscommon line. According to my father, we’re descended from King Niall! Come out and let’s talk!”

No response came. The little people had always been reserved. Nevertheless, without consciously deciding, I realized I needed to speak with them. My mind was blocked by loneliness, preventing me from solving the equation.

If only I could once again hear their dialect and discuss old times, perhaps I could resolve my scientific dilemma.

So I returned to the miniature spaceship and struck it firmly. “Hear me, little people! If you don’t reveal yourselves and speak to me, I’ll destroy this spacecraft!”

Only the leaves responded, rustling softly.

“I’m serious! You have until I count to three! One!”

The glade remained hushed.

“Two!”

I thought I heard a faint crack, as if a twig broke somewhere.

“Three!”

Suddenly, the little people appeared, led by the wizened elder ...

By Vic Phillips and Scott Roberts

"Is that everything, chief? Are you done for the day?"

Brian Hanson shot a look of annoyance at Pete Brent, his tall assistant. It was the first time he'd shown any emotion that day.

"I might be finished, but you aren't," Hanson replied sternly. "Get your records organized. Run the centrifuge tests, and set up the still so we can check the vitamin levels first thing in the morning."

"In the morning? Come on, chief, you should take some time off, maybe even at night. You need to unwind. I know a great blonde you'd like—her name's Myrtle. I have her radiophone number around here somewhere."

Hanson slipped out of his lab coat.

"Forget about Myrtle. Just make sure the equipment is ready. Good night." He left the massive laboratory, his mind still preoccupied with the ongoing vitamin experiments. The comments from his colleagues barely registered.

"One day the chief's going to burn out."

"Not likely," Pete Brent replied.

For a brief moment, Brian Hanson wondered why his team wasn't as engaged with the work as he was. He dismissed the thought as he exited the research facility.

He stopped outside, lifting his gaze to the cluster of buildings around the compound—the administrative core of Venus City. Alone, he allowed himself to feel pride, the only emotion he acknowledged. His position was critical in shaping this burgeoning city. As director of the Venus Consolidated Research Organization, he shouldered much of the responsibility for the planet's growth. Venus Consolidated had developed the city and nearly everything significant on Venus. There were early settlers who had resisted the company's expansion and monopoly, but Hanson believed the company's leadership was best for Venus, and those who disagreed would have to deal with their own misconceptions. Rumors of unrest among the older families had circulated.

He'd heard stories of violence, but thought they were baseless. The Venus Consolidated police were authorized only to make arrests; anything more severe needed approval from the Interplanetary Council on Earth. He dismissed such issues, as he did anything that didn't affect his department directly.

Declining the public transport, Hanson walked to his apartment—an exercise routine he followed to maintain his physical condition despite long hours in the lab. Entering his apartment, he heard water running for his bath, perfectly timed to his walk, which took exactly seven minutes and nearly five seconds. He undressed, sank into the tub, and allowed himself to relax, his mind drifting away from work.

He was suddenly pulled from his reverie by a loud pounding. Dazed, he realized it was the door, not his head, being assaulted. Still wet, he wrapped himself in a towel and shuffled to the door.

"What is it?"

No reply. The knocking persisted.

"Alright, alright! I'm coming!" Hanson shouted, grabbing a towel and crossing the floor with a sound like ducks marching.

Holding the towel, he cautiously opened the door.

"What on earth—" He stopped, surprised to see a police officer.

"Apologies, sir, but a rebel is loose in the Administration Center. We're checking all residences."

"You won't find any rebels here," Hanson said. The officer relaxed, "Of course not, sir. Sorry to bother you. Good night." He left.

Hanson closed the door, puzzled by the officer's smirk. He tried to return to his bath.

As he turned, he was startled. Through the bedroom door, he saw his bed properly made, but a figure under the covers and a cascade of platinum-blonde hair on the pillow were definitely out of the ordinary.

"Hello." The greeting came from a woman whose composed demeanor matched her striking blue eyes. Hanson stared, realizing the policeman’s insinuation.

"Just ask for Myrtle." Pete Brent's teasing suggestion echoed in his mind. He understood now—this must be Brent's idea of a joke.

"Okay, joke's over. Time to leave."

"Joke? The only amusing thing is you and that towel. Either ditch it or get one that fits," she quipped.

Hanson blushed furiously.

"Hand me my robe," he demanded.

The woman stood and Hanson saw she was fully dressed in a fitted overall. He wrapped himself in his robe.

"So, what now?" she asked.

"What do you think? I'm going to finish my bath. You should go keep Pete company in the lab," he snapped. She seemed to be suppressing laughter, which only made him more irritated. He retreated to the bathroom, slamming the door.

The door cracked open.

"Goodbye," she said sweetly. "Say hi to the police for me."

"Get out!" he shouted, and she left, laughing. Hanson grumbled about women and Pete Brent, anticipating extra work for Brent in the lab. He sank back into the bath, determined to let his mind unwind.

Another pounding erupted at the outer door. Hanson groaned, got out of the bath, wrapped himself in his damp robe, and went to the door, angry. He flung it open, ready to confront the intruders, but was interrupted as four police officers and a sergeant rushed in.

Krugman's Life of Brian 

           

                         Where it all started: Paul Krugman's                 "The Legend of Arthur."              

                         Letter from John Cassidy              

         Paul Krugman replies to John Cassidy              

                         Letter from M. Mitchell Waldrop              

         Paul Krugman replies to M. Mitchell Waldrop              

                         Letter from Kenneth J. Arrow              

                         Letter from Ted C. Fishman              

                         David Warsh's July 3, 1994, Boston Globe                              

                                            Letter from John Cassidy:                              

         Paul Krugman loves to berate journalists for their ignorance of economics, particularly his economics, but on this occasion, I fear, his logic is more addled than usual. I am reluctant to dignify his hatchet job with a lengthy reply, but some of his claims are so defamatory that they should be addressed, if only for the record. 

         1) Krugman claims that my opening sentence--"In a way, Bill Gates's current troubles with the Justice Department grew out of an economics seminar that took place thirteen years ago, at Harvard's John F. Kennedy School of Government"--is "pure fiction." Perhaps so, but in that case somebody should tell this to Joel Klein, the assistant attorney general in charge of the antitrust division. When I interviewed Klein for my piece about the Microsoft case, he did not mention Brian Arthur as an influence on his thinking about the way in which high-technology markets operate. It was my own interpretation, not Klein's words, that prompted me to use Arthur in the lead of the story. 

         2) Krugman wrote: "Cassidy's article tells the story of how Stanford Professor Brian Arthur came up with the idea of increasing returns." I wrote no such thing, and Arthur has never, to my knowledge, claimed any such thing. The notion of increasing returns has been around since Adam Smith, and it was written about at length by Alfred Marshall in 1890. What I did say in my article was that increasing returns was largely ignored by mainstream economists for much of the postwar era, a claim that simply isn't controversial. (As Krugman notes, one reason for this was technical, not ideological. Allowing for the possibility of increasing returns tends to rob economic models of two properties that economists cherish: simplicity and determinism. As long ago as 1939, Sir John Hicks, one of the founders of modern economics, noted that increasing returns, if tolerated, could lead to the "wreckage" of a large part of economic theory.) 

         3) Pace Krugman, I also did not claim that Arthur bears principal responsibility for the rediscovery of increasing returns by economists in the 1970s and 1980s. As Krugman notes, several scholars (himself included) who were working in the fields of game theory and international trade published articles incorporating increasing returns before Arthur did. My claim was simply that Arthur applied increasing returns to high-technology markets, and that his work influenced how other economists and government officials think about these markets. Krugman apart, virtually every economist I have spoken to, including Daniel Rubinfeld, a former Berkeley professor who is now the chief economist at the Justice Department's antitrust division, told me this was the case. (Rubinfeld also mentioned several other economists who did influential work, and I cited three of them in the article.) 

         4) Krugman appears to suggest that I made up some quotes, a charge that, if it came from a more objective source, I would consider to be a serious matter. In effect, he is accusing Brian Arthur, a man he calls a "nice guy," of being a fabricator or a liar. The quotes in question came from Arthur, and they were based on his recollections of two meetings that he attended some years ago. After Krugman's article appeared, the Santa Fe professor called me to say that he still recalled the meetings in question as I described them. Krugman, as he admits, wasn't present at either of the meetings. 

         5) For a man who takes his own cogitations extremely seriously, Krugman is remarkably cavalier about attributing motives and beliefs to others. "Cassidy has made it clear in earlier writing that he does not like mainstream economists, and he may have been overly eager to accept a story that puts them in a bad light," he pronounces. I presume this statement refers to a critical piece I wrote in 1996 about the direction that economic research, principally macroeconomic research, has taken over the past two decades. In response to that article, I received dozens of messages of appreciation from mainstream economists, including from two former presidents of the American Economic Association. Among the sources quoted in that piece were the then-chairman of the White House Council of Economic Advisers (Joseph Stiglitz), a governor of the Federal Reserve Board (Laurence Meyer), and a well-known Harvard professor (Gregory Mankiw). To claim, as Krugman does, that I "don't like mainstream economists" and that I am out to denigrate their work is malicious hogwash. The fact of the matter is that I spend much of my life reading the work of mainstream economists, speaking to them, and trying to find something they have written that might interest the general public. In my experience, most economists appreciate the attention. 

         6) I might attach more weight to Krugman's criticisms if I hadn't recently reread his informative 1994 book Peddling Prosperity , in which he devotes a chapter to the rediscovery of increasing returns by contemporary economists. Who are the first scholars Krugman mentions in his account? Paul David, an economic historian who wrote a famous paper about how the QWERTYUIOP typewriter keyboard evolved and, you guessed it, Brian Arthur. "Why QWERTYUIOP?" Krugman wrote. "In the early 1980s, Paul David and his Stanford colleague Brian Arthur asked that question, and quickly realized that it led them into surprisingly deep waters. ... What Paul David, Brian Arthur, and a growing number of other economists began to realize in the late seventies and early eighties was that stories like that of the typewriter keyboard are, in fact, pervasive in the economy." Evidently, Krugman felt four years ago that Arthur's contribution was important enough to merit a prominent mention in his book. Now, he dismisses the same work, saying it "didn't tell me anything that I didn't already know." Doubtless, this change in attitude on Krugman's part is unconnected to the fact that Arthur has started to receive some public recognition. The eminent MIT professor, whose early academic work received widespread media attention, is far too generous a scholar to succumb to such pettiness. 

                         --John Cassidy

The Monster Maker
By RAY BRADBURY
The directive was simple: "Capture Gunther." But the irony was clear—Click and Irish found themselves stranded on a pirate asteroid, armed only with a solitary pistol and a news-reel camera.

[Transcriber's Note: This text is taken from Planet Stories Spring 1944. According to thorough investigation, there is no indication the U.S. copyright for this publication was renewed.]
Without warning, disaster struck. There was no opportunity to react or even feel fear. Click Hathaway, camera loaded and ready, listened to the film spinning rapidly, aware he was documenting extraordinary events as they unfolded.

He caught Marnagan, hunched over the controls, frantically manipulating levers and switches. Beyond them, space glittered with stars, and a meteor approached like a fiery missile.

The ship responded, almost alive under Click’s feet. The meteor collided, crushing the rear jets and sending the vessel into a wild spin, like a celestial carousel.

Noise overwhelmed everything, too much to process. Hathaway was propelled against the control bank, and Marnagan quickly followed, cursing. Through the chaos, Click clung to his camera, determined to capture the meteor’s impact and Marnagan’s desperate efforts.

Suddenly, silence reclaimed the scene. The asteroids seemed to rush closer, cold and relentless. Heart pounding, Hathaway held onto Marnagan, the nearest anchor, as they hurtled toward metallic doom.

"Irish!" he called out. "Is this IT?"

"Is this what?" Marnagan shouted back, helmet muffling his voice.

"Is this when the Big Producer calls CUT!?"

Marnagan bristled. "I’ll die when I choose, and when I do, you can film my profile for Cosmic Films!"

Pressed against the hull, they listened to each other’s harsh breathing.

The ship crashed, bounced, spun, then halted. Both men were tossed around like dice. The hull ruptured, expelling air and energy.

Hathaway screamed, but his mind raced with trivial thoughts—how many moments, like this, never make it to film or audience? His consciousness flickered like the rapid movement of his camera.

Silence consumed the chaos. Hathaway instinctively checked the camera at his belt. All that remained were stars, twisted debris, penetrating cold, and silence. He crawled out of the wreckage, unsure of his actions until he found the camera in his hands, as though it had always belonged there.

He thought, "At least I’ll have some remarkable footage."

A piece of metal toppled, and Marnagan emerged, towering from the debris.

"Freeze!" Hathaway snapped. Marnagan stopped, the camera whirred. "Low angle—Patrolman survives asteroid disaster. Fantastic material. Maybe a pay raise!"

"From my boot!" Marnagan retorted. His shoulders strained inside his suit. "I could have died, and you’re fussing over that camera!"

Hathaway felt a strange pang. "I never considered you might not make it, Irish. I just assumed you’d survive. It’s odd—one tries not to think about dying." He looked at his gloved hand, unable to tell if it was shaking. His face paled. "Where are we?"

"A million miles from anywhere."

They stood on a cratered, ancient meteor surface stretching endlessly beneath a star-studded indigo sky. Above, the sun hung, surrounded by darkness, appearing sickly.

"If we split up, we’d meet on the other side in two hours," Marnagan said, shaking his dusty red hair. "I promised Luna Base I’d catch Gunther this time."

His words faded, replaced by silence.

Hathaway’s heart pumped anxiously. "I checked my oxygen—sixty minutes left."

Silence emphasized the situation. Among the sharp rocks, Hathaway saw the destroyed radio and scattered food. Their escape was lucky—or was suffocation a kinder fate?
Sixty minutes.
They faced each other.

"Damn that meteor!" Marnagan exclaimed.

Hathaway remembered something. "Someone directed that meteor, Irish. I filmed it, saw it up close—it was blazing hot. Genuine space rocks aren’t hot or glowing. If you want proof, it’s on film."

Marnagan grimaced. "We need oxygen first, Click. Then food. Then a way home."

Hathaway continued, "This is Gunther’s doing. He’s probably nearby, enjoying his handiwork. If we ever return to Earth, this would make sensational news—Irish Marnagan, victim of an unseen pirate, Gunther, triumphs at last. Filmed by me, Click Hathaway. Cosmic Films, take note."

They moved quickly across the rugged terrain toward a jagged metallic ridge, alert and searching. Anything was better than waiting.

Marnagan said, "We’re on borrowed time, and only your suspicion separates us from death. We have fifty minutes to prove it wasn’t an accident. After that, right or wrong, you’ll be Cosmic Films’ most impressive but lifeless genius. Talk as much as you want, Click. In moments like this, words matter. You have your camera and your story. As for me," he twisted his red face, "survival is my passion. I didn’t sign up for this kind of death."

Click nodded. "Gunther knows you’d hate dying this way, Irish. That’s why he orchestrated the meteor and crash."

Marnagan said nothing, lips tense, green eyes blazing.

They halted together.

"Wait!" Click said.

"Did you feel that?" Marnagan blinked.

Hathaway suddenly felt light, almost weightless. "Irish! We lost weight crossing that ridge!"

They retraced their steps. "Let’s try again."

They repeated the experiment, puzzled. "Gravity shouldn’t behave like this, Click."

"You’re telling me? It’s artificial. No—it's Gunther! We fell so quickly—pulled down by enhanced gravity! Gunther would do anything—did I say anything?"

THE GREAT NEBRASKA SEA
By ALLAN DANZIG

 Illustrated by WOOD

 [Transcriber's Note: This etext was produced from Galaxy Magazine August 1963.
 Extensive research did not uncover any evidence that the U.S. copyright on this publication was renewed.]
It has happened a hundred times in the long history of Earth—and, sooner or later, will happen again!
Everyone—all the geologists, at any rate—had known about the Kiowa Fault for years. That was before there was anything very interesting to know about it. The first survey of Colorado traced its course north and south in the narrow valley of Kiowa Creek about twenty miles east of Denver; it extended south to the Arkansas River. And that was about all even the professionals were interested in knowing. There was never so much as a landslide to bring the Fault to the attention of the general public.

 It was still a matter of academic interest when in the late '40s geologists speculated on the relationship between the Kiowa Fault and the Conchas Fault farther south, in New Mexico, and which followed the Pecos as far south as Texas.

 Nor was there much in the papers a few years later when it was suggested that the Niobrara Fault (just inside and roughly parallel to the eastern border of Wyoming) was a northerly extension of the Kiowa. By the mid sixties it was definitely established that the three Faults were in fact a single line of fissure in the essential rock, stretching almost from the Canadian border well south of the New Mexico-Texas line.

 It is not really surprising that it took so long to figure out the connection. The population of the states affected was in places as low as five people per square mile! The land was so dry it seemed impossible that it could ever be used except for sheep-farming.

 It strikes us today as ironic that from the late '50s there was grave concern about the level of the water table throughout the entire area.
The even more ironic solution to the problem began in the summer of 1973. It had been a particularly hot and dry August, and the Forestry Service was keeping an anxious eye out for the fires it knew it could expect. Dense smoke was reported rising above a virtually uninhabited area along Black Squirrel Creek, and a plane was sent out for a report.

 The report was—no fire at all. The rising cloud was not smoke, but dust. Thousands of cubic feet of dry earth rising lazily on the summer air. Rock slides, they guessed; certainly no fire. The Forestry Service had other worries at the moment, and filed the report.

 But after a week had gone by, the town of Edison, a good twenty miles away from the slides, was still complaining of the dust. Springs was going dry, too, apparently from underground disturbances. Not even in the Rockies could anyone remember a series of rock slides as bad as this.

 Newspapers in the mountain states gave it a few inches on the front page; anything is news in late August. And the geologists became interested. Seismologists were reporting unusual activity in the area, tremors too severe to be rock slides. Volcanic activity? Specifically, a dust volcano? Unusual, they knew, but right on the Kiowa Fault—could be.

 Labor Day crowds read the scientific conjectures with late summer lassitude. Sunday supplements ran four-color artists' conceptions of the possible volcano. "Only Active Volcano in U. S.?" demanded the headlines, and some papers even left off the question mark.

 It may seem odd that the simplest explanation was practically not mentioned. Only Joseph Schwartzberg, head geographer of the Department of the Interior, wondered if the disturbance might not be a settling of the Kiowa Fault. His suggestion was mentioned on page nine or ten of the Monday newspapers (page 27 of the New York Times). The idea was not nearly so exciting as a volcano, even a lava-less one, and you couldn't draw a very dramatic picture of it.

 To excuse the other geologists, it must be said that the Kiowa Fault had never acted up before. It never sidestepped, never jiggled, never, never produced the regular shows of its little sister out in California, which almost daily bounced San Francisco or Los Angeles, or some place in between. The dust volcano was on the face of it a more plausible theory.

 Still, it was only a theory. It had to be proved. As the tremors grew bigger, along with the affected area, as several towns including Edison were shaken to pieces by incredible earthquakes, whole bus- and plane-loads of geologists set out for Colorado, without even waiting for their university and government department to approve budgets.

 They found, of course, that Schwartzberg had been perfectly correct.
They found themselves on the scene of what was fast becoming the most violent and widespread earthquake North America—probably the world—has ever seen in historic times. To describe it in the simplest terms, land east of the Fault was settling, and at a precipitous rate.

 Rock scraped rock with a whining roar. Shuddery as a squeaky piece of chalk raked across a blackboard, the noise was deafening. The surfaces of the land east and west of the Fault seemed no longer to have any relation to each other. To the west, tortured rock reared into cliffs. East, where sharp reports and muffled wheezes told of continued buckling and dropping, the earth trembled downward. Atop the new cliffs, which seemed to grow by sudden inches from heaving rubble, dry earth fissured and trembled, sliding acres at a time to fall, smoking, into the bucking, heaving bottom of the depression.

 There the devastation was even more thorough, if less spectacular. Dry earth churned like mud, and rock shards weighing tons bumped and rolled about like pebbles as they shivered and cracked into pebbles themselves. "It looks like sand dancing in a child's sieve," said the normally impassive Schwartzberg in a nationwide broadcast from the scene of disaster. "No one here has ever seen anything like it." And the landslip was growing, north and south along the Fault.

 "Get out while you can," Schwartzberg urged the population of the affected area. "When it's over you can come back and pick up the pieces." But the band of scientists who had rallied to his leadership privately wondered if there would be any pieces.

 The Arkansas River, at Avondale and North Avondale, was sluggishly backing north into the deepening trough. At the rate things were going, there might be a new lake the entire length of El Paso and Pueblo Counties. And, warned Schwartzberg, this might only be the beginning.

Land west of the Fault was holding firm, though Denver had recorded several small tremors; everywhere east of the Fault, to almost twenty miles away, the now-familiar lurch and steady fall had already sent several thousand Coloradans scurrying for safety.

 All mountain climbing was prohibited on the Eastern Slope because of the danger of rock slides from minor quakes. The geologists went home to wait.

 There wasn't much to wait for. The news got worse and worse. The Huerfano River past Cedarwood was creating a vast mud puddle where the town of Cedarwood had been. Just below Masters, Colorado, the river leaped 70-foot cliffs to add to the heaving chaos below. And the cliffs were higher every day as the land beneath them groaned downward in mile-square gulps.

ALL DAY SEPTEMBER
By ROGER KUYKENDALL
Art by van Dongen
[Editor’s Note: This document is based on Astounding Science Fiction, June 1959. Research has found no evidence of a U.S. copyright renewal.]
Some individuals simply lack common sense. They’re unable to grasp the most basic truths—like when it’s time to accept defeat and stop trying against all odds....
A meteor, no bigger than a match head, had traveled for eons through the universe. The star that perished to create this meteor illuminated Earth well before the earliest life forms left the oceans.

At the end of its journey, the meteor landed on the Moon, colliding with Evans’ tractor in the process.

It punctured the steam turbine’s outer shell, vaporizing itself and parts of the turbine blades on impact. The turbine, spinning at eight thousand revolutions per minute, lost equilibrium. The shaft contorted, and damaged blades were ejected through the casing. Eventually, the turbine stabilized—in a permanent stop.

Evans found himself two days away from lunar sunrise.

Meanwhile, evening was approaching in Sydney, Australia, and the terminator—the line between night and day—was visible on the Moon’s surface, creeping across Australia.

Without a wristwatch, Evans estimated the time as a quarter past Australia.

Evans worked as a prospector—part amateur geologist or, more accurately, selenologist. His tractor and gear were worth $250,000, with $50,000 paid and the balance covered by loans and shares. When funds were low, which was often, he hauled uranium ore and metallic sodium from Potter’s Dike mines to Williamson Town, the rocket port.

When he had some cash, he’d go prospecting for a few weeks. He once chased a rush to Yellow Crater, believing he’d found rich chromite, but the deposit ran out after only six weeks, and he barely broke even.

At the time of the accident, Evans was about three hundred miles east of Williamson Town, the Moon’s original landing site.

He was due back in Williamson Town by sunset, roughly sixteen days away. Observing his ruined turbine, Evans immediately realized he wouldn’t return in time. Careful rationing could allow his food to stretch beyond a month. His supply of drinking water—stored separately from reactor water—might also last as long. But his oxygen reserves were strictly measured: four days’ supply, with the possibility of stretching it an extra day through careful use. Counting this reserve plus his normal supply (sixteen days), Evans calculated he had twenty-one days to survive.

He might be missed after seventeen days, but by then, the lunar night would have returned. Any search would be delayed another thirteen days, making rescue at least eight days too late.

“Well, Evans, you’ve landed yourself in quite a predicament,” he muttered.

“Let’s see just how dire things are,” he replied to himself. Fumbling for the light switch, he found it already on.

“The batteries must be drained,” he reasoned.

“What batteries? There aren’t any here. The power comes from the generator.”

“So why isn’t the generator running?”

After some thought, he recalled the generator was powered by a small reciprocating engine—not the main turbine—but it still required steam from the same boiler, which had emptied due to the breach in the turbine. The condenser, too—

“The condenser!” he exclaimed.

Using a small flashlight, he examined the steam system and discovered about three gallons of ice in the condenser. Like all condensers, this one converted steam back into water for reuse in the boiler. It included a tank and coiled pipes inside a reflective enclosure radiating heat into space. After the meteor punctured the turbine, water in the condenser boiled away, lowering the temperature until the remaining water froze.

Evans isolated the turbine by closing shut-off valves. If any water remained in the boiler, it could power the generator via the engine. Condensed steam would return to the boiler if the ice in the condenser melted and the pump wasn’t jammed.

But the boiler was dry. Cautiously, Evans poured a cup of drinking water into the boiler’s intake, sealed it, and flipped the “Nuclear Start/Safety Bypass” lever. The water flashed into steam, briefly spinning the generator.

When the lights flickered and died, Evans realized the issue.

“There’s not enough water to thaw the ice in the condenser,” he noted.

He opened the pipe again, this time using nearly half a gallon of his precious water—a quantity that could have lasted three days if rationed. For someone with only a month’s supply and just over twenty days to live, it was a significant sacrifice.

The generator restarted, and the lights came back. They flickered as pressure dropped, but some ice had melted, and the water pump resumed operation.

“At least I’ll have light to die by,” he sighed.

Sunrise arrived at Williamson Town about when it did for Evans. The disk of the sun blazed intensely against the black lunar sky, with stars shining nearby as if the sun weren’t present. The only distortion was from solar flares, but no one risked looking directly at the sun without filters.

Director McIlroy entered his office, already brightened by morning sunlight. The glare was so strong it pushed into the room’s deepest shadows. He drew the polaroid shade to its darkest, turning the sun a deep reddish-brown and dimming the room. Adjusting the shade for comfort, he found the air stuffy and decided to leave his inner office door open.

He hesitated, recalling his rule that all doors remain closed except during passage, to maintain air conditioning and minimize air loss in the event of an unlikely meteor strike. Still, he consoled himself—he was no more lenient with his own rules than anyone else on the survey team.

McIlroy doubted his abilities as a leader. In fact, he thought himself entirely unsuited for leadership. His strictest orders were routinely ignored, yet his gentlest suggestions were met with enthusiasm.

Everyone else on the team saw this clearly, but McIlroy accepted it without much reflection. He’d grown accustomed to making suggestions for things he truly wanted done, and issuing orders he was indifferent about.

For instance, an order prohibiting alcohol in the survey building ensured a steady supply of homemade spirits for all.

COMPLEXITY AND HUMANITY
We have all seen the images. Volunteers pitching in. People working day
 and night; coming up with the most ingenious, improvised solutions to
 everything from food and shelter to communications and security. Working
 together; patching up the fabric that is rent. Disaster, natural or
 otherwise, is a breakdown of systems. For a time, chaos reigns. For a
 time, what will happen in the next five minutes, five hours, and five
 days is unknown. All we have to rely on are our wits, fortitude, and
 common humanity
Contemporary life is not chaotic, in the colloquial sense we apply to
 disaster zones. It is, however, complex and rapidly changing; much more
 so than life was in the past; even the very near past. Life, of course,
 was never simple. But the fact that day-to-day behaviors in Shenzhen and
 Bangalore have direct and immediate effects on people from Wichita to
 Strasbourg, from Rio de Janeiro to Sydney, or that unscrupulous lenders
 and careless borrowers in the United States can upend economic
 expectations everywhere else in the world, no matter how carefully
 others have planned, means that there are many more moving parts that
 affect each other. And from this scale of practical effects, complexity
 emerges. New things too were ever under the sun; but the systematic
 application of knowledge to the creation of new knowledge, innovation to
 innovation, and information to making more information has become
 pervasive; and with it the knowledge that next year will be very
 different than this. The Web, after all, is less than a generation old.
These two features−the global scale of interdependence of human action,
 and the systematic acceleration of innovation, make contemporary life a
 bit like a slow motion disaster, in one important respect. Its very
 unpredictability makes it unwise to build systems that take too much
 away from what human beings do best: look, think, innovate, adapt,
 discuss, learn, and repeat. That is why we have seen many more systems
 take on highly structured, command-and-control models in the last decade and a half: from the consolidation of Toyota’s production system with the highly structured model put in place by Henry Ford, to the Internet’s shift toward centrally managed protocols, and on to the way Wikipedia enforces strict editorial oversight and hierarchical approval for knowledge contributions—processes that would have been seen, until recently, as too rigid ever to scale (and are still seen so by many). But it is time we acknowledge that systems work best by achieving consistency through structure.
Modern Times
Modern times were hard enough. Trains and planes, telegraph and
 telephone, all brought many people into the same causal space. The
 solution to this increased complexity in the late 19th, early 20th
 century was to increase the role of structure and improve its design.
 During the first two-thirds of the twentieth century, this type of
 rationalization took the form of ever-more complex managed systems, with
 crisp specification of roles, lines of authority, communication and
 control.
In business, this rationalization was typified by Fredrick Taylor’s
 Scientific Management, later embodied in Henry Ford’s assembly line. The
 ambition of these approaches was to specify everything that needed doing
 in minute detail, to enforce it through monitoring and rewards, and
 later to build it into the very technology of work−the assembly line.
 The idea was to eliminate human error and variability in the face of
 change by removing thinking to the system, and thus neutralizing the
 variability of the human beings who worked it. Few images captured that
 time, and what it did to humanity, more vividly than Charlie Chaplin’s
 assembly line worker in Modern Times.
At the same time, government experienced the rise of bureaucratization
 and the administrative state. Nowhere was this done more brutally than
 in the totalitarian states of mid-century. But the impulse to build
 fully-specified systems, designed by experts, monitored and controlled
 so as to limit human greed and error and to manage uncertainty, was
 basic and widespread. It underlay the development of the enormously
 successful state bureaucracies that responded to the Great Depression
 with the New Deal. It took shape in the Marshall Plan to pull Europe out
 of the material abyss into which it had been plunged by World War II,
 and shepherded Japan’s industrial regeneration from it. In technical
 systems too, we saw in mid-century marvels like the AT&T telephone
 system and the IBM mainframe. For a moment in history, these large scale
 managed systems were achieving efficiencies that seemed to overwhelm
 competing models: from the Tennessee Valley Authority to Sputnik, from
 Watson’s IBM to General Motors. Yet, to list these paragons from today’s
 perspective is already to presage the demise of the belief in their
 inevitable victory.
The increasing recognition of the limits of command-and-control systems

This retrenchment, not an abandonment, of the goal of perfect rationalization of systems design, assumed much of the human away. What replaced perfect-market planning in these systems was a renewed emphasis on structured control. This was achieved through a hyper-simplification of human nature, wedded to mathematical modeling of what hyper-simplified selfish rational actors, looking only to their own interests, would do under diverse conditions. This approach was widespread and influential; it still is. And yet it led to such unforgettable gems as trying to understand why people do, or do not, use condoms by writing sentences like: “The expected utility (EU) of unsafe sex for m and for f is equal to the benefits (B) of unsafe sex minus its expected costs, and is given by EUm = B - C(1-Pm)(Pf) and EUf = B - C(1-Pf)(Pm),” and believing that you will learn anything useful about lust and desire, recklessness and helplessness, or how to slow down the transmission of AIDS. Only by concocting such a thin model of humanity−no more than the economists’ utility curve−and neglecting any complexities of social interactions that could not be conveyed through prices, could the appearance of rationalization be maintained. Like bureaucratic rationalization, perfect-market rationalization also had successes. But, like its predecessor, its limits as an approach to human systems design are becoming clear.

Pricing perfectly requires perfect information. And perfect information,

Not that there aren’t human-centric practices. And not that either of these approaches to coordinating human action will disappear.
